newsitem.title: UK: Market share of U.K. petrol sites outlined - study.
newsitem.headline: Market share of U.K. petrol sites outlined - study.

text.p: British petrol station closures almost doubled in 1996 from the previous year, even as supermarket sites continued to grow and the average amount of fuel sold at each station increased from 1995, according to the Institute of Petroleum (IP).
Tesco Plc held the most sites among the supermarkets with 273, followed by J. Sainsbury Plc with 189 and Safeway Plc with 138, the IP, a trade group, said in its 1997 UK Retail Marketing Survey.
Esso, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, was the U.K. leader with 1,980 sites, followed by Royal Dutch/Shell Group with 1,706 and British Petroleum with 1,289, IP said.

"With the intense level of competition in the market today, the lower margin environment will not change and the focus will remain on the active management of the cost base to squeeze every drop of value out of every pound spent..." John Adkins, retail division manager of Esso Petroleum, said in the report.
The total number of sites that closed last year was 1,496, nearly double the rate of 1995 to leave total filling stations at 14,478, IP said. That is down sharply from 20,641 in 1986.

The sharp rise in site closures was attributed primarily to Esso's Pricewatch campaign launched in early 1996, the growing presence of the low-cost supermarkets who increased their number of sites by 6.5 percent, and a chronic overcapacity in the U.K., analysts said.

"One thing is certain, the eight pence/litre margin of yesterday will not be seen again, and, hopefully, neither will the two pence/litre days of 1996," J. Attwood, director of retail marketing at Total Oil Great Britain, was quoted as saying.
The average U.K. price for four-star petrol in 1996, with taxes accounting for 78-80 percent of the total cost, was 61.40 pence per litre, up from 59.12 pence the previous year, IP said.

Repsol's retail manager R.K. Thompson said that "market conditions reached an all-time low in 1996. The battle for market share preservation became 'God' for the refiners, all hell bent on volume protection at any cost."

"It is almost certain that restructuring is not complete and that 1997 will see more changes -- more closures and, maybe, more joint ventures," said J. Attwood, director of retail marketing at Total Oil Great Britain.
